Indeed, it passes all understanding, my dear Charlotte, how a young man of Mr. Thornton's apparent good breeding could behave with such a want of principle! To make such devoted attentions to a girl as amiable and accomplished as Miss Eleanor Beaumont, and then, at the very first breath of a larger fortune, to quite cast her off! It is beyond belief, I assure you.

His conduct, Mrs. Everleigh, has certainly occasioned much surprise; though I confess, I had ever held some slight apprehension regarding the constancy of his character. He possessed, I thought, a certain volatility of temper which might, under trying circumstances, sway him from the path of honour.

Volatility, you call it, my dear? I call it a plain lack of proper feeling! Why, I remember him quite hanging upon her every word at the Assembly just last month, and dancing with none but her for half the evening. And now, within a fortnight, he is to be seen riding in Miss Finch’s phaeton, and complimenting her dreadful taste in ribbons! Lord, it makes one quite despair of the young men of today. When there is money to be had, they quite forget everything else, every promise, every sentiment! And Miss Finch, they say, has forty thousand pounds at her own disposal; a sum which, I fear, must quite eclipse any virtues Miss Beaumont may possess in the eyes of a man so mercenary.

Miss Finch, then, is indeed so wealthy?

Wealthy, my dear, she is absolutely laden with it! Her grandmother, old Lady Finch, was known to be quite the miser, and left all her immense fortune to this one grandchild, who, I might add, is no beauty, nor particularly clever. But forty thousand pounds! It is a fortune that would make any plain face appear radiant, and any dull wit seem keen, to a gentleman in Mr. Thornton’s present circumstances. For they say his own affairs are much disordered; his father, the late Sir Richard, though a man of excellent family, was never one to deny himself, and the estate, I understand, is sadly encumbered. No wonder he so hastily abandoned poor Eleanor; he was, I suppose, quite desperate for such a settlement.

I had heard some whispers of his embarrassments, but knew not they were so pressing. Yet, that can be no true excuse for such unfeeling behaviour. A man of honour, however straitened his circumstances, would surely not seek to mend his fortune by breaking a young lady’s heart and reputation.

A man of honour, indeed! Where are such men to be found now-a-days, Charlotte? You speak of a time long past, I fear. These young gentlemen, they will have their pleasures, their hunters, their carriages, and their London seasons; and when the money runs short, they simply look about for the nearest heiress. It is a scandalous state of affairs, and I say it is quite a pity that more parents do not instill proper principles in their sons. But then, parents are often as eager for a good match as their offspring, are they not?

There is truth in your observation, ma’am, I will not deny it. But for Miss Beaumont, I confess, my heart aches. She is a girl of such gentle spirit and delicate health. I dread to think how she will bear this blow.

Poor dear Eleanor! I have sent her a little dish of my own apricot cordial; it is excellent for the nerves, you know. I sincerely hope it may offer her some small comfort. Though what comfort can truly heal such a wound, I cannot imagine! It is a dreadful thing for a girl, such a disappointment; it quite ruins her prospects, does it not? For who will look at a girl who has been so publicly slighted, even if it is not her fault?

I trust, Mrs. Everleigh, that her many virtues, and the general esteem in which her family is held, will prevail over such ungenerous speculation. Miss Beaumont possesses a character of true worth, which must, in time, be properly appreciated.

Let us hope so, my dear, let us sincerely hope so. But the world is a cruel place, is it not? And people will talk. I have no doubt that Mrs. Thompson, with her sharp tongue, will make much of this little drama. She hinted to me only yesterday, that she always thought Mr. Thornton was 'too dashing' to be quite steady. As if that were a judgement on Eleanor! It is all very unfair, and I shall take care to contradict her most roundly, should she bring the matter up again. One must protect the innocent, you know.

Your kindness, ma’am, is ever to be admired. Have you any notion how Miss Beaumont received the intelligence?

Oh, my dear, most dreadfully, I hear! Mrs. Davison, who is her aunt, came to me this very morning, quite in despair. Eleanor, she said, had taken to her bed, and would see no one. She had not eaten a morsel, nor spoken a word, since Mr. Thornton’s formal note of dismissal arrived. A cold, formal little note, Mrs. Davison assured me, quite devoid of any real regret, and full of vague excuses about 'unforeseen difficulties' and 'a change in prospects'. As if he were merely cancelling an engagement to ride, and not dashing the hopes of a trusting young woman! I declared to Mrs. Davison that I thought it a most shocking piece of impertinence, and quite enough to make one quite ill oneself, merely to hear of it.

Indeed, it is. I had hoped Mr. Thornton might at least have had the grace to call upon her, and to express his sentiments in person, however painful such a duty might prove.

Call upon her? Bless you, Charlotte! He has no such scruples. He is already too deep in Miss Finch’s good graces, and no doubt fears her displeasure, should he show any lingering attention to his former flame. And Miss Finch, I hear, is a jealous creature; quite possessive of her forty thousand pounds, and of any gentleman who might aspire to them. No, no, Mr. Thornton will not risk his new found comfort for the sake of an old acquaintance, however dear. But tell me, my dear, for you are so clever at such things, what do you think will become of poor Eleanor? Will she ever recover from such a disappointment?

With time, ma’am, and the affection of her family and friends, I have every hope she will. She is possessed of much fortitude, though it may not always be evident in moments of such acute distress. And her understanding, I trust, will guide her to accept that a heart so easily swayed by fortune is not one deserving of her continued regard.

Well spoken, my dear, most excellently spoken. But still, it is a hard thing for a girl to bear. I remember my own sister, poor Eliza, who was slighted by a Captain Fairfax; she never quite recovered her spirits, and eventually married a clergyman older than her father, merely for a home! But then, Eliza was always of a weaker constitution. Eleanor, perhaps, is made of sterner stuff. Let us trust in Providence, and perhaps a little diversion might help. My niece, Fanny, is coming to tea this afternoon, and she has promised to bring her new music. Perhaps if we could persuade Eleanor to join us, the music might take her mind from her sorrows for a little while?

That is a most thoughtful suggestion, Mrs. Everleigh, but I doubt she will be prevailed upon. I think, perhaps, her best remedy for the present is quiet reflection and the solitude of her own chamber. I shall, if you will permit me, call upon her this evening, and offer what little comfort I may; though I shall certainly not press her to join us.

Aye, aye, you are quite right, my dear; solitude it must be for a time. But then, too much solitude is never good, is it? One begins to brood, and to imagine things. And what good does that ever do, I ask you? I do hope she will soon see that Mr. Thornton, with his fickle heart, was never worthy of her; and then, perhaps, she may turn her thoughts to worthier gentlemen. There is young Mr. Davies, from the Grange, who has always admired her, and has a very handsome property; though perhaps not quite so dashing as Mr. Thornton. And then there is Mr. Fitzwilliam, who is a most solid and respectable man, though perhaps a little too fond of his books. But a good fortune, and a kind disposition, are surely more to be valued than a pretty face or a fashionable curricle, are they not? And a solid two thousand a year, without debt or encumbrance, is not to be sniffed at, I assure you.

Indeed, ma'am, a kind disposition is above all price. But for now, I believe Miss Beaumont requires only peace. And with a gentle inclination of her head, Miss Selwyn rose. She would call upon Eleanor, and sit with her in silence, which, she knew, often spoke more eloquently than the most well-intended words. She hoped that her friend might, in time, come to understand the true nature of Mr. Thornton's character, and see his departure not as a loss, but as a providential escape.

“Dear Ma’am,” said Miss Selwyn, taking the glass of wine with a polite smile, though she felt a considerable weariness settle upon her own spirits. “You are too good, but I do not think Eleanor will be disposed to drink it. She has little inclination for any comfort just now, save perhaps the quiet of her own thoughts, however painful they may be. And I confess, I think it best not to press her.”

Mrs. Jennings, for it was indeed she, though here named Mrs. Everleigh by the narrator’s pleasantry, looked at the glass, then at Miss Selwyn, and then sighed. “Ah, well, it is excellent Constantia, I assure you; many a time has my poor husband declared it a sovereign remedy for every ill, from a fit of the gout to a fit of the vapours. But if she will not, she will not, and there is an end to it. Such obstinacy is what I always say about young people; they will have their own way, even in their suffering. Do you know, I offered my Eliza the very same in her trouble, and she poured it all, every drop, down the drain, declaring it tasted of physic! Well, it is no matter. I shall drink it myself then, for it is a pity to waste good wine, and after all this talking I feel quite parched.”

With a shrug of her ample shoulders, Mrs. Jennings settled herself into a large armchair near the fire, which Miss Selwyn had recently left, and, with a cheerful gulp, consumed a good portion of the Constantia. Miss Selwyn, however, felt a greater duty called her back to Eleanor’s chamber, not for the purpose of administering wine, but simply to be present, a silent witness to her friend’s distress. She knew well that true sympathy often lay in quiet companionship, not in a bustling attempt to distract or cheer. Eleanor, she was certain, required no more than to feel herself not utterly abandoned to her grief, yet left unmolested by the well-meaning, though often burdensome, efforts of others.

Upon reaching the chamber once more, Miss Selwyn found Eleanor exactly as she had left her, still leaning over the dying embers, her head bowed low. The only change was the increasing gloom of the evening, which had deepened the shadows in the room and rendered Eleanor’s form even more indistinct against the fading light. Miss Selwyn drew a chair quietly to a little distance, not so near as to intrude upon the private anguish, yet close enough to convey her presence. She sat down, and for a long while, no word was spoken. The only sounds were the soft settling of the house for the night, the distant murmurs from the drawing-room where Mrs. Jennings was no doubt holding forth, and, occasionally, a faint, almost imperceptible tremor that ran through Eleanor’s frame.

It was a delicate balance, this art of comforting a grieving friend. Too much solicitude could be oppressive; too little, negligent. Miss Selwyn chose the path of silent vigilance, allowing Eleanor the space to grieve without feeling the pressure to perform cheerfulness, or even to speak. She watched the fire slowly yield its last sparks, and the room grow colder, until at last she rose to lay another log upon the hearth. The sudden flicker of light roused Eleanor a little, for she stirred and lifted her head, her eyes, though still swollen and red, meeting Miss Selwyn’s with a look of profound weariness.

“You are still here, Catherine?” Eleanor’s voice was a mere whisper, thin and fragile.

“Yes, my dear,” Miss Selwyn replied softly, her hand resting for a moment on Eleanor’s shoulder. “I did not wish to leave you quite alone. And it is growing cold in here; the fire needed mending.”

Eleanor merely nodded, a long, drawn-out sigh escaping her lips. “I am a poor companion tonight, Catherine. I am fit for no society, not even yours.”

“You need not be a companion, Eleanor, nor do I require company,” Miss Selwyn assured her. “Only rest, if you can find it. Do you think you might be persuaded to go to bed? It is late, and you have had a trying day.”

“To bed?” Eleanor repeated, a faint, bitter smile touching her lips. “And what comfort will bed bring? Only more hours for my mind to wander over what might have been, and what now is. Sleep is a kindness I do not deserve, perhaps, for having allowed myself to be so foolish.”

“Folly, my dear, is a common failing of human nature, especially when the heart is engaged,” Miss Selwyn said gently. “But it is not one that deserves such suffering as yours. You have been betrayed, not foolish, and a proper indignation, once your strength returns, will do you more service than this self-reproach.”

Eleanor did not respond to this, but turned her gaze back to the newly kindled flames, her expression still lost in sorrow. Miss Selwyn knew it was useless to press further. Grief, like a fever, must run its course. She resumed her seat, and the quiet vigil continued, a testament to a friendship that needed no words to communicate its depth.

After another period of silence, which seemed to stretch interminably, a discreet tap came at the door. Miss Selwyn, rising quietly, opened it to find Fanny, Mrs. Jennings’s niece, standing in the passageway, a sheet of music clutched in her hand, her pretty, eager face alight with a mixture of apprehension and youthful curiosity.

“Oh, Miss Selwyn, I beg your pardon, I did not mean to disturb you,” Fanny whispered, her eyes darting past Miss Selwyn to the shadowed room within. “Aunt Everleigh sent me to see if Eleanor would perhaps come down. We have tea, and I have brought my new piece; it is a lively waltz, quite the fashion, and I thought it might amuse her.”

Miss Selwyn smiled kindly at the young girl. Fanny was a good-hearted creature, if a little thoughtless in her vivacity, and entirely devoid of malice. “Thank you, Fanny, it is very good of you, and of your aunt. But I fear Eleanor is not yet ready for company, nor for music, however charming. She requires perfect quiet just now. Perhaps another evening, when her spirits are somewhat mended.”

Fanny’s face fell a little. “Oh, dear. Aunt Everleigh did say she was very sad, but I had hoped the music… well, never mind. I shall tell Aunt Everleigh. I hope she feels better soon.” With a final, sympathetic glance towards the room, Fanny departed, her light footsteps echoing faintly down the corridor.

Miss Selwyn closed the door once more and returned to Eleanor. “Fanny came to inquire,” she said, knowing Eleanor had heard. “She offered her music.”

Eleanor merely shook her head, a gesture of profound weariness. “No, Catherine. No music, no company. Only this. This heavy emptiness.”

“Then this it shall be for now,” Miss Selwyn agreed, and again silence descended, broken only by the crackle of the fire and the measured beat of their two hearts, one burdened by sorrow, the other by a quiet, steady sympathy. It was not until the clock on the mantelpiece struck nine that Eleanor, with a sudden, weary movement, pushed herself upright.

“I believe, Catherine,” she said, her voice still weak, “I shall attempt to sleep now. You are right; I am much fatigued. Perhaps a few hours of oblivion may grant me some respite from this cruel reflection.”

Miss Selwyn helped her friend to rise, and with gentle persuasion, assisted her into bed. She then sat by the bedside until Eleanor’s breathing grew regular, a soft, even rhythm that bespoke the arrival of a troubled, yet merciful, slumber. It was a small victory, yet a victory nonetheless. Miss Selwyn then quietly extinguished the lamp, leaving Eleanor to the darkness and such peace as sleep might bring, and returned to the drawing-room.

She found Mrs. Jennings still ensconced by the fire, a teacup in one hand, the other gesturing emphatically as she conversed with Fanny, who sat opposite her, trying her best to appear attentive.

“Ah, there you are, my dear Miss Selwyn!” Mrs. Jennings exclaimed upon Miss Selwyn’s entrance. “Is she abed then? Poor soul, it is the best place for her. Nothing like a good sleep to put things right, though I always found a little of my husband’s Constantia worked wonders too. Fanny here has been telling me all about her new waltz; it is quite pretty, she says, but I told her, what Eleanor wants now is not a waltz, but a good husband, a steady one, with a solid income. That Mr. Thornton, indeed! A mere flirt, a popinjay! Always dashing about, spending more than he has, I’ll warrant. No real stability there. And Miss Grey, with her fifty thousand pounds, will soon find that out, I dare say, if she is not too enamoured of his pretty face to see sense. But then, young women are always taken in by a handsome exterior, are they not? Lord, I was myself once, until my good husband, rest his soul, taught me the true value of a substantial fortune and a good temper. And if Eleanor had only listened to me, she would have seen through Mr. Thornton straight away. I told her not a month ago, when he was paying her such marked attention, that he was too flighty, too fond of his own pursuits, to make a constant partner. But no, she would not hear it.”

Miss Selwyn listened to this torrent of words with a patient smile, knowing that interruption was futile, and indeed, often counterproductive. Mrs. Jennings, in her volubility, usually exhausted herself sooner if left unhindered.

“Well,” Mrs. Jennings continued, taking a hearty sip of tea, “as I was saying to Fanny, now that Mr. Thornton has shown his true colours, Eleanor is free, and a very desirable young woman she is, despite this little setback. She has beauty, she has accomplishments, and though her fortune is not so great as some, it is very respectable indeed. And she has always been much admired, has she not, Fanny?”

Fanny, startled by the sudden address, stammered, “Oh, yes, Aunt, indeed she has. Everyone always said she was the prettiest girl in the county.”

“There, you see!” Mrs. Jennings affirmed, beaming at her niece. “And now, with this experience, she will be wiser, more discerning. She will know what to look for in a man. Not a handsome face, not a dashing equipage, but good sense, good principles, and above all, a good solid establishment. And I have just the man in mind, my dear Miss Selwyn, for I was thinking of him all the time you were upstairs. Mr. Davies, from the Grange. He is a most worthy young man. Always admired Eleanor, I know it for a fact. And his property, though not quite so grand as some, is in excellent order, and he has a comfortable two thousand pounds a year, clear of all encumbrance, as I heard from old Mr. Jenkins, who manages his affairs. He is a little reserved, perhaps, a little bookish, but that is no bad thing, for it means he will be a quiet, constant husband, and not running off to London every season, throwing away his money on trifles. And he has always been very kind to Eleanor, very respectful. I believe he would make her an excellent partner, indeed I do. What do you say, Miss Selwyn? Do you not agree?”

Miss Selwyn chose her words carefully, for to outright contradict Mrs. Jennings was to invite a prolonged and often heated debate. “Mr. Davies is, as you say, ma’am, a very respectable gentleman, and indeed, his character is universally esteemed. But I think, for the present, Eleanor needs no thought of any gentleman, be he ever so worthy. Her heart is too bruised, her spirits too low, to entertain such considerations. Time, and quiet reflection, are her only remedies just now.”

“Oh, time, time, yes, of course, time is a great healer,” Mrs. Jennings conceded, though with an impatient wave of her hand. “But one cannot let the grass grow under one’s feet, Miss Selwyn. Opportunities, you know, do not wait for grief to subside. And when a young woman is once disappointed, it can cast a long shadow over her prospects, unless she is quickly brought forward again. And Mr. Davies, as I say, has always been very sweet on Eleanor. I think I shall invite him to tea tomorrow. Just a quiet tea, you understand, no fuss. He will be calling on his aunt, Mrs. Jenkins, who lives just down the lane, so it will be no trouble for him to step across. What do you think, Fanny? Would that not be a good idea?”

Fanny, always eager to please, readily agreed. “Oh, yes, Aunt, I think it would be excellent! Mr. Davies is very good, and he does play the flute rather well, though not so well as Mr. Henderson.”

“Nonsense, child, the flute is neither here nor there,” Mrs. Jennings declared, dismissing Fanny’s observation with another wave. “It is the solid worth of the man that matters. And a pleasant face, of course; he is not ill-favoured, is he, Miss Selwyn?”

“He is certainly not,” Miss Selwyn replied, a faint smile playing on her lips. “He is a man of pleasing address and appearance.” She inwardly resolved to find a discreet way to deter Mr. Davies, should he indeed be invited, or at least to ensure that Eleanor remained in her room, safely sequestered from any premature introduction to a new suitor. The thought of Eleanor being paraded before a prospective husband in her current state was quite unbearable.

The conversation then drifted to other topics, mostly local gossip and domestic arrangements, with Mrs. Jennings holding court and Fanny interjecting occasionally with girlish observations. Miss Selwyn, while listening with an air of polite attention, allowed her mind to wander to Eleanor’s plight. She reflected upon the strange intricacies of human affections, how easily a heart could be captivated, and how painfully it could be dashed. Mr. Thornton, with his superficial charms and evident lack of principle, had inflicted a wound that would take long to heal. It was a lamentable truth that young women, especially those of warm sensibility like Eleanor, were often susceptible to outward show, mistaking a lively manner for a benevolent heart, and careless attention for genuine attachment. Miss Selwyn had always prided herself on her own discernment, though she acknowledged that even the keenest observer could be misled by artful dissimulation.

As the evening wore on, and the clock chimed ten, Miss Selwyn rose to take her leave. “I think I shall retire now, ma’am,” she said to Mrs. Jennings. “It has been a long day, and I too feel the need of rest.”

“To be sure, to be sure, my dear,” Mrs. Jennings assented, rousing herself with a contented sigh. “A very sensible plan. And do not trouble yourself about Eleanor; she will be better in the morning, I warrant you. A good night’s sleep, and perhaps a little something strengthening for breakfast, and she will feel quite a different creature. And tomorrow, we shall see Mr. Davies. Who knows, a new face might be just the thing to put the old one quite out of her head.”

Miss Selwyn merely offered another polite smile, knowing it was useless to argue. She bade Fanny goodnight, and then made her way to her own chamber, her thoughts still preoccupied with Eleanor’s sorrow. She hoped sincerely that sleep would indeed bring some peace to her friend, and that the morning light, however unwelcome, would find Eleanor with a renewed, if fragile, sense of fortitude. The path to recovery would be long and arduous, but Miss Selwyn was determined to walk it with her friend, offering strength and solace where she could, and steadfastly guarding her from the well-intentioned but often clumsy efforts of others.

The next morning, Miss Selwyn rose early, her sleep having been less undisturbed than she might have wished, for Eleanor’s pale face and tear-stained eyes had frequently visited her dreams. She dressed quickly and made her way to Eleanor’s room, eager to ascertain her friend’s state. Mr. Palmer says they cost a great deal of money to feed, but I tell him it is worth it, for they take us everywhere! The afternoon wore on, a tedious progression of forced cheerfulness and strained conversation. Mrs. Jennings, utterly convinced of the efficacy of her plan, darted about the room, attempting to draw Marianne into conversation, or to make her smile.

“Marianne, my dear, Mr. Harris is playing your favourite tune! You used to dance to that one at Norland, did you not? Oh, to be young again! Come, tell us, what do you think of this music?”

Marianne would offer a barely audible, “It is very pleasant, Mrs. Jennings,” or a faint shake of her head, and retreat into herself once more. Elinor would then subtly deflect Mrs. Jennings’s attention, or engage her in another topic, sparing Marianne the effort of further response. She watched her sister closely, noting the tremors in her hand when she occasionally reached for a cup of tea, the increasing pallor of her cheeks, and the determined blankness of her expression. It was evident that every moment was an effort, a struggle to maintain a semblance of composure for the sake of propriety and to spare Elinor further anxiety.

The Miss Steeles, unburdened by any deep understanding of Marianne’s sorrow, or indeed, any sorrow beyond their own trivial disappointments, continued to chatter about London fashions, their acquaintances, and their hopes of marrying well. Their conversation, though innocent, was a jarring counterpoint to the quiet tragedy unfolding in the corner of the room. Lucy, in particular, occasionally glanced at Elinor, as if attempting to gauge her reaction to some piece of gossip, or perhaps, to assess her own standing in the household. Elinor, though weary, maintained her usual calm and polite demeanour, revealing nothing of her inner disquiet.

As the light began to fade, and the candles were brought in, casting a softer glow upon the scene, Mr. Harris concluded his musical performance. He then offered to read aloud from a volume of poetry, a proposal which Mrs. Jennings enthusiastically endorsed, believing it another excellent means of diversion. Elinor inwardly groaned, fearing that poetry, the very fuel of Marianne’s romantic sensibility, would either plunge her deeper into despair or, by its poignant beauty, force a painful eruption of emotion.

Mr. Harris, with a pleasant if uninspired voice, began to read a passage from Thomson’s *Seasons*. His chosen lines, descriptive of the melancholy beauty of autumn, and the solitude of nature, were, to Elinor’s dismay, perfectly calculated to exacerbate Marianne’s present state. She watched as Marianne’s rigid posture seemed to soften, her eyes now fixed on Mr. Harris, absorbing every word with an intensity that boded ill. A tear, slow and unnoticed by the others, trickled down her cheek. Elinor knew she had to intervene.

“Mr. Harris,” she said gently, interrupting him at the close of a particularly evocative stanza, “that is a most beautiful passage, but I fear my sister finds herself a little overcome by such tender sentiments this evening. Perhaps a lighter subject, or indeed, a little more music, might be more agreeable to her spirits.”

Mrs. Jennings, ever quick to agree when a direct hint was given, though often blind to the subtle signs of distress, exclaimed, “Indeed, indeed! Elinor is quite right! We must have something more cheerful! No sad poetry, Mr. Harris, if you please! Play us another jig! Or perhaps, Sir John, you could tell us one of your amusing anecdotes? You always have so many diverting stories!”

Sir John, delighted to be called upon, readily launched into a humorous tale of a fox hunt gone awry, his booming laugh and exaggerated gestures drawing the attention of most of the company. Marianne, thus momentarily released from the emotional torment of the poetry, looked gratefully at Elinor, though she made no direct acknowledgement.

At length, to Elinor’s profound relief, the evening began to draw to a close. Mrs. Palmer, after a final burst of laughter at one of Sir John’s jokes, declared that Mr. Palmer would be quite impatient if they stayed out much longer. Sir John, after urging Mrs. Jennings to dine with them the following day, bade everyone a hearty goodnight. The Miss Steeles, after lingering a little longer, exchanging promises of future visits with Mrs. Jennings, at last took their leave, Lucy casting a final, lingering glance at Elinor, as if to ascertain something she had not yet discovered. Mr. Harris bowed politely, collected his flute, and departed.

The instant the door closed behind the last guest, Marianne rose from her chair, her face a mask of exhaustion and despair. “Elinor,” she said, her voice trembling, “I can bear no more. I must go to my room.”

Mrs. Jennings, however, intercepted them, her face glowing with satisfaction. “Well, now, was not that a charming evening! And did I not tell you, Marianne, my dear, that a little company would do you good? You look quite revived! Not so pale now, are you? And you were quite composed! They mean only kindness, however clumsy their expression of it may be. Try to rest now, my love. Forget the evening. You have done all that was required of you, and you may now give way to your sorrow in private, without fear of interruption. I shall stay with you for a little while.”

Marianne clutched Elinor’s hand, her tears flowing silently. “You are always so good, Elinor. So strong. How do you bear it? How do you maintain such composure when everything within you must be raging?”

Elinor sighed, a deep, weary breath that she had held within her throughout the long afternoon. “It is an art I have been forced to learn, Marianne, for both our sakes. She remained by Marianne’s side until her sister’s sobs subsided into a fitful slumber, her breathing uneven. She felt a profound weariness, not merely physical, but a spiritual exhaustion born of the constant vigilance and the suppression of her own emotions. The well-meaning but utterly insensitive nature of Mrs. Jennings and her guests had made an already painful situation almost unbearable for Marianne, and Elinor had felt the keen edge of every thoughtless remark and every misplaced attempt at cheer.

Her heart ached for Marianne, whose transparent sincerity rendered her so vulnerable to the world’s indifference. Elinor, by contrast, possessed a greater degree of fortitude and self-command; yet, even her own equanimity had been severely tested by the protracted ordeal. She reflected on Mrs. Palmer’s blundering mention of Willoughby, and the Miss Steeles’s superficial chatter, and Sir John’s boisterous, unthinking jests. All had been offered with the best intentions, yet all had inflicted fresh wounds upon a spirit already bleeding. It was a cruel irony, she thought, that such genuine kindness could be so entirely devoid of true understanding.

She knew that Mrs. Jennings, delighted with the success of her “diversion,” would undoubtedly plan further entertainments, convinced that she was providing the very medicine Marianne required. Elinor foresaw a succession of equally trying evenings, a constant battle against the encroachment of well-meaning but intrusive company, and the necessity of perpetual guardianship over Marianne’s delicate state. It was a prospect that filled her with dread, for she knew that to truly recover, Marianne needed time, solitude, and perhaps, the quiet solace of her own thoughts, however painful they might be. Elinor could only brace herself for the trials to come, resolved to protect her sister with every ounce of her strength and discretion. Her own feelings, her own private grief over Marianne’s suffering, had to be suppressed, for there was no one to confide in, no one to share the burden. She was Marianne’s sole comfort, her only shield against a world that, in its eagerness to be kind, often inflicted the most unintended cruelties. The night brought no immediate solace to Elinor; she too lay awake for a long while, listening to the quiet sounds of the house, and praying for strength to face the morrow.

Marianne remained in her room, utterly exhausted from the previous evening's exertion, and Elinor did not press her to descend for breakfast. She conveyed to Mrs. Jennings, with a polite but firm tone, that Marianne required a day of absolute quiet, and that any further company would be detrimental to her recovery. Mrs. Jennings, though initially inclined to protest, was swayed by Elinor’s earnest assurances that Marianne had indeed found the previous evening beneficial, but now needed to consolidate her gains through rest.

“Well, if you think so, my dear,” Mrs. Jennings conceded, though with a sigh of regret. “I had thought of sending for Colonel Brandon again, for he is such a steady, sensible man, and always so pleased to see Marianne. But perhaps another day will do. We must not overdo it. You know best, my dear, of course. She is your sister, after all. But I must say, I am quite convinced that a little society is the best thing in the world for low spirits. And our little party yesterday was quite charming, was it not? The Miss Steeles are such lively girls, and Mr. Harris plays the flute divinely. I dare say Marianne felt quite cheered by it all, in spite of herself. Indeed, I saw a little colour in her cheeks when Sir John was telling that story about the overturned chaise. She must have been laughing inside, you know, even if she did not show it!”

Elinor offered a vague, non-committal smile, recognizing the futility of correcting Mrs. Jennings’s benevolent misapprehensions. To disillusion her would only cause offence, and gain no advantage for Marianne. She merely reiterated that quietude was now essential, and Mrs. Jennings, with a final, lingering expression of doubt, turned her attention to the household arrangements, and the planning of future, equally “beneficial” diversions.

Yet, these considerations, pressing as they were, could not distract her from the immediate and overwhelming priority: Marianne’s life.

Colonel Brandon, observing Elinor’s momentary lapse into troubled thought, gently placed a hand upon her arm. “You must rest, Miss Dashwood,” he said, his voice unusually soft. “Even for an hour. Mrs. Allen and I will watch her. You are exhausted.”

“I cannot,” Elinor replied, shaking her head. “Not while Marianne is in such peril. I must be here.”

He did not press her further, understanding, perhaps, that her own torment would not allow her to leave her sister’s side. He merely nodded, and continued his silent vigil, his gaze fixed upon Marianne, his concern as palpable as Elinor’s own. The quiet dignity of his sorrow touched Elinor deeply. She knew he had long harboured a deep affection for Marianne, an affection that Marianne, in her youthful vivacity, had perhaps never fully appreciated, or indeed, deserved. Now, in this dark hour, his devotion shone forth with a quiet, enduring light.

The sun was high in the sky, casting long, pale shadows across the floor, when Marianne at last stirred with a greater degree of consciousness. Her eyes opened, slowly but with more focus, and she looked about the room, her gaze resting first on Elinor, then on Colonel Brandon, then on Mrs. Allen, a flicker of confusion crossing her face.

“Elinor?” she whispered, her voice a mere thread of sound. “What has… what has happened?”

Elinor sank to her knees beside the bed, tears springing to her eyes. “Oh, Marianne, my dearest sister! You have been very ill. Do not try to speak too much now. Only rest.” She gently stroked Marianne’s hair, her heart overflowing with a mixture of immense relief and lingering fear. The danger was not yet past, but the darkest hours, she prayed, were now behind them.

Colonel Brandon stepped forward, a faint, almost imperceptible smile of relief touching his lips. “You are awake, Miss Marianne. That is well. We have had a trying night.”

Marianne frowned slightly, a confused expression upon her face, as if she were trying to recall something elusive from a troubled dream. She tried to lift her hand to her head, but it fell back weakly. “My head aches,” she murmured. “I feel so… so strange.”

“You have been very unwell, my love,” Elinor reiterated. “But you are better now. We must still be very careful.”

Dr. Harris returned shortly after, and upon examining Marianne, pronounced himself cautiously optimistic. “The crisis appears to have passed, Miss Dashwood. Her pulse is stronger, and she is fully conscious, though much weakened. She must be kept quiet, and take only broth for a day or two. But with continued care, I believe she will recover.”

The words were like music to Elinor’s ears, lifting a burden from her heart that she had not fully realised the extent of. She looked at Colonel Brandon, and their eyes met in a moment of shared, profound relief. In that instant, Elinor knew a gratitude that surpassed all conventional expressions. He had been their anchor in the storm, his steadfast strength the very foundation upon which Marianne’s fragile life now seemed to rest.

Elinor remained by Marianne’s side throughout the day, watching over her, speaking to her in low tones, and ministering to her every need. Colonel Brandon, having ensured that all was in order, and that Mrs. Allen was settled comfortably with instructions for Marianne’s care, excused himself to attend to some pressing matters, promising to return later in the evening. His departure left a quiet void in the room, yet Elinor was too relieved, too emotionally spent, to truly notice, her focus now entirely upon her sister.

Marianne drifted in and out of sleep, her weakness profound, but each awakening brought a clearer gaze, a more coherent word. As the day wore on, she began to remember fragments of the previous night, though the details remained hazy, blurred by the powerful effects of the opiate. She asked Elinor, in a weak voice, about the phial, about her mother’s medicine, and Elinor, though still uncertain how best to frame the truth, gently reassured her that all would be explained when she was stronger.

The evening brought Mrs. Jennings, who, having been discreetly informed of Marianne’s sudden, severe indisposition, arrived with a flurry of worried questions, her usual boisterous manner subdued by genuine concern. Elinor, mindful of Marianne’s fragile state, offered only the most general explanations, attributing her sister’s illness to a sudden fever and chill. Mrs. Jennings, though her sharp eyes clearly suspected more than was being told, respected Elinor’s reticence, and settled for expressing her sympathy and her hopes for Marianne’s swift recovery, while also offering a thousand practical suggestions for broths and poultices. She spoke in hushed tones, however, which was a mercy, for Elinor could scarcely have borne her usual effusions.

Later, when Marianne had again fallen into a restorative sleep, Elinor found a moment to step out of the room, seeking a brief respite from the close atmosphere. She descended to the drawing-room, where she found Colonel Brandon quietly seated by the fire, a book open upon his lap, though he was not reading. He looked up as she entered, his expression one of quiet inquiry.

“She is sleeping now,” Elinor reported, her voice still low. “A more natural sleep, I believe. Dr. Harris says she will recover, with care.”

A look of immense relief, deeper and more profound than Elinor had ever seen, crossed Colonel Brandon’s face. He closed his book, placing it aside. “Thank God,” he said, the words barely audible, yet laden with heartfelt emotion. “It has been a terrible night, Miss Dashwood.”

“Indeed it has, Colonel,” Elinor agreed, sinking into a chair opposite him, feeling the full weight of her exhaustion. “And I do not know how I could have endured it without you. Your promptness, your presence of mind, your unwavering support… I am indebted to you beyond words.”

He looked at her, his dark eyes conveying an earnest sincerity that warmed her weary heart. “There is no debt, Miss Dashwood. My only desire was to see Miss Marianne safe. And for you, to be spared such a trial alone.” He paused, then continued, his voice gentle. “You have borne yourself with remarkable fortitude throughout this dreadful affair. Your strength of character is truly admirable.”

Elinor felt a blush rise to her cheeks at his praise, unused as she was to such direct expressions of admiration. She merely inclined her head in acknowledgment, unable to find words to express the complicated emotions that welled within her. The shared ordeal had forged a new understanding between them, an unspoken recognition of strength and reliability. She saw him not merely as Marianne’s admirer, but as a man of profound honour, of quiet courage, and of a steadfast goodness that was, in truth, a far more precious quality than any superficial charm.

“We must consider what is to be said, Colonel,” Elinor began, after a brief silence, her thoughts turning to the difficult task of explaining Marianne’s condition. “My mother will need to be informed, and soon.”

Colonel Brandon nodded gravely. “Indeed. We must act with great discretion, Miss Dashwood. For Miss Marianne’s sake, and for the family’s honour, this matter must remain as private as possible.” He looked into the fire, a thoughtful expression on his face. “I shall be ready to assist in any way I can. Perhaps, with Dr. Harris’s help, a plausible explanation of a sudden fever or a severe nervous attack might suffice for the general ear. The true cause, I believe, should be confined to ourselves, and to Mrs. Dashwood.”

“You are right, of course,” Elinor said, a wave of weariness washing over her. “And for Marianne herself, when she is stronger… we must address the circumstances that led to this lamentable event.” She knew, with a sinking heart, that the true cause lay in the cruel desertion of Mr. Willoughby, and that the revelation of his character would be a difficult and painful subject to broach with her sister. But for now, the immediate danger had passed, and for that, Elinor offered a silent, heartfelt prayer of thanks. The path ahead was still fraught with difficulties, but at least, for this night, Marianne had been snatched from the very brink.
